name: Gunther von Hagens
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: invented plastination in 1977 at age 32; at age 26 (1971) he was completing medical studies after escaping East Germany. No material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in German-annexed Poland in 1945, von Hagens grew up in East Germany and began medical studies at the University of Jena in 1965. He was imprisoned for attempting to flee East Germany in 1969, escaped to West Germany in 1970, and completed his medical degree at the University of Lübeck in 1973. He invented plastination at Heidelberg in 1977 at age 32.
family_context_summary: Born Gunther Gerhard Liebchen; father was a member of the SS and later a coal industry supervisor. Family fled westward from the Red Army when von Hagens was five days old, settling in East Germany. He was a haemophiliac and spent six months in hospital as a child.
evidence_summary: Von Hagens began medical studies at 20 and completed his doctorate at 30, but his signature invention of plastination came at age 32 in 1977. No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 was found. His early life was marked by haemophilia, political imprisonment, and escape from East Germany.

name: James May
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: fame arrived at age 40 with Top Gear in 2003; at age 26 (1989) he was working various entry-level jobs after university. No material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in Bristol to an aluminium factory manager, May studied music at Lancaster University and spent a year at technical college learning metalwork. After graduating, he worked at a car dealership, a jewellery shop, the NHS, and the London Underground, getting fired from most jobs. He later found work as a sub-editor at The Engineer magazine before moving into automotive journalism at Autocar.
family_context_summary: Son of an aluminium factory manager and a homemaker; one of four children. Grew up in a middle-class household in Wales and South Yorkshire.
evidence_summary: May described himself as a late developer with no vision or ambition as a young man. He worked a series of unremarkable jobs after university and did not achieve notable success until joining Top Gear at age 40. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Richard Hughes
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Keane's breakthrough single 'Somewhere Only We Know' reached No. 3 in the UK charts in 2004 when Hughes was 29; at age 26 (2001) the band was still unsigned and playing small venues. No material milestone by 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born in Gravesend, Kent, Hughes attended Tonbridge School where he met future Keane bandmates Tim Rice-Oxley and Dominic Scott. He learned drums at age 17 and joined their covers band in 1995. He studied geography at UCL and worked as a BBC secretary to support himself while the band practiced in a London flat. Keane did not achieve commercial success until 2004.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Attended Tonbridge School, a selective independent school, suggesting a middle-to-upper-middle-class background.
evidence_summary: Hughes started drums late at 17 and joined Keane at 20, but the band remained unsigned and obscure through his mid-20s. Their commercial breakthrough came in 2004 when he was 29. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Kim Milton Nielsen
milestone_by_age_26: Became a Danish top-flight football referee by his mid-20s (approximately 1985-86), an unusually early achievement for a national-level referee.
early_history_summary: Born in Copenhagen, Nielsen began refereeing at age 15 in 1975 after taking a referee course at his local football club. A decade later, while still in his mid-20s, he was officiating Danish top-flight matches. He received his FIFA international badge in 1988 at age 28 and went on to referee 154 internationals and 53 UEFA Champions League games.
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Worked as an IT manager alongside his refereeing career.
primary_early_advantage_tags: early refereeing start, Danish FA pipeline, physical height advantage, direct football immersion
evidence_summary: Nielsen started refereeing at 15 and reached the Danish top flight by his mid-20s, an unusually rapid rise. He benefited from the Danish FA referee development system and his imposing 1.96m height. His major international appointments (FIFA badge, Champions League finals) came after age 26, but reaching top-flight domestic refereeing by 25-26 is a material career milestone.
starting_point: Born in Copenhagen, Denmark; family background not documented in reviewed sources; worked as an IT manager alongside refereeing.
current_position: Retired from refereeing in 2006 after reaching the FIFA age limit of 45; had officiated 154 internationals and 53 Champions League games including the 2004 Champions League final.

trajectory.event: Passed referee exam and began officiating matches in Denmark.
Reached Danish top-flight refereeing level, an unusually early achievement.
Awarded FIFA international referee badge.
Received first major UEFA call-up for the UEFA Super Cup.
Appointed to referee the UEFA Cup final.
Refereed the UEFA Champions League final between Porto and Monaco.
Retired from refereeing after reaching the FIFA age limit.

name: Pavel Sheremet
milestone_by_age_26: Became editor-in-chief of Belorusskaya Delovaya Gazeta and ORT Minsk bureau chief in 1995-96, and was arrested in July 1997 for an investigative border-crossing report that sparked an international incident between Belarus and Russia.
early_history_summary: Born in Minsk, Sheremet worked in a bank's foreign exchange department until 1992 before becoming a consultant for economic programs on Belarusian TV. From 1994 to 1995 he anchored the weekly news program Prospekt on Belarus state TV until it was banned by Lukashenko. He then became editor-in-chief of Belorusskaya Delovaya Gazeta and ORT's Minsk bureau chief. In July 1997, his arrest for filming an illegal border crossing sparked an international incident.
family_context_summary: Born in Minsk, Belarus (then part of the Soviet Union). Came to journalism from banking, starting in 1992 as a consultant for economic programs on Belarusian television. Family financial background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: post-Soviet media opening, state TV platform, ORT bureau chief, authoritarian repression as catalyst
evidence_summary: Sheremet pivoted from banking to journalism at 21 and quickly rose to anchor a state TV news program by 23. After Lukashenko banned his program, he became editor-in-chief of a major business newspaper and ORT's Minsk bureau chief by 24-25. His 1997 arrest for investigative journalism sparked an international incident, making him a globally recognized figure by 26. The authoritarian repression of Belarusian media was both his defining challenge and the source of his prominence.
starting_point: Born in Minsk, Belarus (then Soviet Union); came to journalism from a banking career, starting as a TV consultant on economic programs in 1992.
current_position: Killed by a car bomb in Kyiv on 20 July 2016 at age 44; was a prominent journalist working with Ukrainian Pravda and a CPJ International Press Freedom Award winner.

trajectory.event: Became anchor and producer of Prospekt, a weekly news program on Belarus state TV.
Became editor-in-chief of Belorusskaya Delovaya Gazeta and began working for Russian ORT television.
Named ORT Minsk bureau chief, covering Belarus for Russian public television.
Arrested for filming an illegal border crossing report, sparking an international incident between Belarus and Russia.
Awarded the CPJ International Press Freedom Award.
Awarded the OSCE Prize for Journalism and Democracy.
Created the Historical Truth website and began writing for Ukrainian Pravda.
Killed by a car bomb in Kyiv on 20 July 2016.

name: Chen Jingrun
milestone_by_age_26: Presented results on Tarry's problem at the National Mathematical Paper Conference in Beijing in August 1956 (age 23), recognized by renowned mathematician Hua Luogeng, and joined the Institute of Mathematics at the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 1957; published first paper in Acta Mathematica Sinica in 1958.
early_history_summary: Born to a poor postal worker's family in Fuzhou, Fujian, Chen endured the Second Sino-Japanese War as a child and lost his mother to tuberculosis at age 14. A high school teacher, Shen Yuan, inspired him with Goldbach's Conjecture. He graduated from Xiamen University in 1953 at age 20, briefly taught at a middle school, then returned to Xiamen as a librarian in 1955. He independently improved on Hua Luogeng's work on Tarry's problem, leading to his recruitment to the Chinese Academy of Sciences in 1957.
family_context_summary: Son of a postal worker in a poor family of twelve children. Endured the Second Sino-Japanese War as a refugee child and lost his mother to tuberculosis at age 14. The family lived in horrific wartime circumstances.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a postal clerk and later post office director. No family background in mathematics or academia documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Hua Luogeng mentorship, Shen Yuan inspiration, CAS pipeline, wartime adversity, obsessive concentration
evidence_summary: Chen grew up in extreme poverty during wartime China, losing his mother at 14. A high school teacher inspired him with Goldbach's Conjecture, and at Xiamen University he was nicknamed 'Einstein' by classmates. He independently improved on Hua Luogeng's number theory work while working as a librarian, studying even in air raid shelters. Hua recognized his talent and brought him to the Chinese Academy of Sciences at age 24. His obsessive concentration and mentorship from Hua were the key accelerants despite complete absence of family resources.
starting_point: Born to a poor postal worker's family of twelve children in Fuzhou, Fujian, China; endured the Second Sino-Japanese War as a refugee child and lost his mother to tuberculosis at age 14.
current_position: Died on 19 March 1996 at age 62 in Beijing; was a mathematician at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, famous for Chen's theorem on Goldbach's Conjecture.

trajectory.event: Graduated from the Mathematics Department of Xiamen University.
Presented results on Tarry's problem at the National Mathematical Paper Conference in Beijing, recognized by Hua Luogeng.
Joined the Institute of Mathematics at the Chinese Academy of Sciences on Hua Luogeng's recommendation.
Published first paper 'On Waring's problem for n-th powers' in Acta Mathematica Sinica.
Announced Chen's theorem: every sufficiently large even number is the sum of a prime and a semiprime.
Published the full proof of Chen's theorem after surviving persecution during the Cultural Revolution.
Xu Chi's biography 'Goldbach's Conjecture' made Chen a national celebrity in China.
Died on 19 March 1996 in Beijing after years of declining health from brain injuries and Parkinson's disease.

name: Sandra Izbașa
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold on floor exercise at the 2008 Beijing Olympics at age 18, and won a second Olympic gold on vault at the 2012 London Olympics at age 22.
early_history_summary: Born in Bucharest to medical assistant parents, Izbașa started gymnastics at age 4 in 1994 at CSS Steaua Bucharest. She joined the Romanian national team in 2002 at age 12. At 16, she won gold on floor at the 2006 European Championships and bronze in the all-around at the 2006 World Championships. She won Olympic floor gold at 18 in Beijing 2008 and vault gold at 22 in London 2012.
family_context_summary: Born in Bucharest, Romania; father Florin Nicolae and mother Roxana Daniela were both medical assistants. Started gymnastics at age 4 at CSS Steaua Bucharest.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were medical assistants; no family background in gymnastics or athletics documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Romanian gymnastics system, Steaua Bucharest, early start at 4, national team at 12, elite coaching
evidence_summary: Izbașa benefited from Romania's world-class gymnastics pipeline, starting at Steaua Bucharest at age 4 and joining the national team at 12. She was coached by elite national team coaches including Octavian Bellu and Mariana Bitang. By 16 she was winning European gold; by 18, Olympic gold. Her entire childhood was immersed in elite gymnastics training, with no documented family domain advantage but strong institutional support from the Romanian gymnastics system.
starting_point: Born in Bucharest, Romania to parents who were both medical assistants; started gymnastics at age 4 at CSS Steaua Bucharest.
current_position: Retired from competitive gymnastics in April 2014 at age 24; double Olympic champion (2008 floor, 2012 vault) with five European Championship golds.

trajectory.event: Joined the Romanian national gymnastics team.
Won gold on floor at the European Championships and bronze in all-around at the World Championships.
Won Olympic gold on floor exercise at the Beijing Olympics.
Won gold on floor and vault at the European Championships after recovering from a torn Achilles tendon.
Won Olympic gold on vault at the London Olympics.
Retired from competitive gymnastics in April 2014.

name: Anna Dogonadze
milestone_by_age_26: Won a gold medal with the Soviet team at the 1990 World Championships at age 17, and won synchro gold at the 1993 World Cup Final and 1998 World Championships.
early_history_summary: Born in Mtskheta, Georgia, Dogonadze was introduced to trampoline by her grandmother as a small child. She rose through the Soviet gymnastics system and won World Championship team gold with the Soviet Union in 1990 at age 17. After Georgia's independence, she competed for Georgia, winning World Cup Final synchro gold in 1993. She moved to Germany in 1998, became a German citizen, and won World Championship synchro gold that same year.
family_context_summary: Born in Mtskheta, Georgia (then Soviet Union). Her grandmother introduced her to trampoline as a small child. She moved to Germany in 1998 for personal reasons (marriage to her former coach), leaving her family behind in Georgia.
parent_family_domain_summary: Grandmother introduced her to trampoline gymnastics at a very young age in Georgia, which was the entry point to her entire career. No further family domain background documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet gymnastics system, grandmother introduction, early childhood start, World Championship at 17, migration to Germany
evidence_summary: Dogonadze was introduced to trampoline by her grandmother as a toddler and benefited from the Soviet Union's elite gymnastics pipeline. She won World Championship team gold at 17 in 1990. After the Soviet collapse, she competed for Georgia before moving to Germany in 1998, where she continued her career at the highest level. Her early childhood immersion in trampoline through the Soviet system was the dominant advantage, with no documented family financial resources.
starting_point: Born in Mtskheta, Georgia (then Soviet Union); grandmother introduced her to trampoline as a small child; rose through the Soviet gymnastics system.
current_position: Retired from competitive trampoline after the 2012 Olympics; works as a sports teacher, coach, and personal trainer in Bad Kreuznach, Germany; 2004 Olympic champion and four-time World champion.

trajectory.event: Won gold medal with the Soviet team at the World Championships and placed sixth individually.
Won gold in synchro event at the World Cup Final competing for Georgia.
Won bronze medal in the individual event at the World Games.
Moved to Germany, won World Championship synchro gold alongside Tina Ludwig.
Won her first individual world title at the World Championships.
Won Olympic gold medal in individual trampoline at the Athens Olympics.
Competed in her fourth consecutive Olympics at London, her final major competition.

name: Baldur Preiml
milestone_by_age_26: Won a Four Hills Tournament round in Bischofshofen in January 1964 at age 24, finished third overall in the tournament, and won gold at the Winter Universiade in February 1964.
early_history_summary: Born to a mountain farming family in Greifenburg, Carinthia, Preiml initially competed in track and field (Carinthian decathlon champion) before being discovered for ski jumping by Siegi Kostner of WSG Radenthein. He became Austrian youth champion in ski jumping at 18 in 1958 and joined the national team at 20 in 1959. His breakthrough came in 1964 with a Four Hills Tournament round win and Universiade gold, followed by an Olympic bronze at Grenoble in 1968.
family_context_summary: Son of a Carinthian mountain farming family in Greifenburg, Austria. Grew up in an Alpine farming community with no documented financial advantages.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in ski jumping documented. Father was a mountain farmer.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Carinthian Alps, ski jumping culture, Kostner discovery, Austrian national team, decathlon athleticism
evidence_summary: Preiml grew up in a Carinthian mountain farming family, immersed in Alpine ski jumping culture from childhood. He was discovered by Siegi Kostner of WSG Radenthein and became Austrian youth champion at 18. His geographic immersion in Austria's ski jumping heartland was the dominant advantage, complemented by natural athleticism (Carinthian decathlon champion). He had no family financial resources but benefited from the Austrian national team pipeline and local ski jumping infrastructure.
starting_point: Born to a Carinthian mountain farming family in Greifenburg, Austria; grew up in an Alpine farming community in the heart of Austrian ski jumping country.
current_position: Died on 27 January 2025 at age 85 in Spittal an der Drau, Carinthia; was a former Olympic bronze medalist and head coach who revolutionized Austrian ski jumping as the 'father of the Austrian ski jumping miracle.'

trajectory.event: Became Austrian youth champion in ski jumping.
Joined the Austrian senior national ski jumping team.
Won a Four Hills Tournament round in Bischofshofen, finished third overall, and won gold at the Winter Universiade.
Won Olympic bronze medal on the normal hill at the Grenoble Winter Olympics.
Became head coach of the Austrian national ski jumping team, pioneering mental training and nutrition methods.
Became manager of the sport section of the Austrian Federal Ministry of Education, Arts and Sport.
Died on 27 January 2025 in Spittal an der Drau, Carinthia.

name: Nando Parrado
milestone_by_age_26: Survived the 1972 Andes plane crash (Uruguayan Air Force Flight 571) and, alongside Roberto Canessa, completed a 10-day trek through the Andes mountains to find help, rescuing the remaining 16 survivors after 72 days.
early_history_summary: Born in Montevideo to a comfortable family in the affluent Carrasco neighborhood, Parrado attended Stella Maris College and played rugby for Old Christians Club. At age 22, he was a university business student when his rugby team's flight crashed in the Andes on 13 October 1972. After 72 days of survival, he and Roberto Canessa trekked for 10 days through the mountains to find rescue. The story was told in the 1974 bestseller 'Alive' and a 1993 film.
family_context_summary: Born in Montevideo, Uruguay, the second of three children. Father Seler Parrado owned hardware stores and was president of the Uruguayan Racing Drivers Association. Mother Xenia was a Ukrainian immigrant. Grew up in the affluent Carrasco neighborhood.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Andes survival, team cohesion, affluent family background, rugby community, extreme adversity
evidence_summary: Parrado came from a comfortable Montevideo family; his father owned hardware stores and led the racing drivers association. He attended Stella Maris College and played rugby for Old Christians Club, a tight-knit community. The 1972 Andes crash was an extreme adversity that catalyzed his defining life story. His survival and 10-day trek with Canessa demonstrated extraordinary mental fortitude and teamwork. No particular domain expertise or early career milestone preceded the crash; his fame derives entirely from the survival event.
starting_point: Born in Montevideo, Uruguay to a comfortable family in the affluent Carrasco neighborhood; father owned hardware stores and was president of the Uruguayan Racing Drivers Association; mother was a Ukrainian immigrant.
current_position: President of MRC Ltda, a television production company in Uruguay; renowned motivational speaker and author; 76 years old as of 2025.

trajectory.event: Survived the Andes plane crash and spent 72 days stranded in the mountains.
Completed a 10-day trek through the Andes with Roberto Canessa to find rescue for the remaining survivors.
The bestseller 'Alive' by Piers Paul Read told the story of the survival and rescue.
Served as technical advisor for the film 'Alive,' portrayed by Ethan Hawke.
Published memoir 'Miracle in the Andes: 72 Days on the Mountain and My Long Trek Home.'
Continues as president of MRC Ltda and active motivational speaker.

name: Jan Železný
milestone_by_age_26: Broke the javelin throw world record with 87.66m in Nitra on 31 May 1987 at age 21, and won bronze at the 1987 World Championships in Rome; won Olympic silver at the 1988 Seoul Olympics at age 22.
early_history_summary: Born in Mladá Boleslav, Czechoslovakia, both of Železný's parents were javelin throwers. His father Jaroslav was his coach at AŠ Mladá Boleslav. He won the Czechoslovak junior title at 17 in 1983 and debuted internationally at the European Junior Championships. He committed fully to athletics after watching the 1983 World Championships. He joined the military sports club Dukla Banská Bystrica and broke the world record at 21 in 1987.
family_context_summary: Born prematurely in the seventh month of pregnancy weighing 2.3 kg with a retracted left foot. Both parents were javelin throwers (father Jaroslav: 68.46m personal best, mother Jana: 43.23m). Father became his coach. Older brother Peter also threw javelin.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents competed in javelin throw; father Jaroslav served as Jan's coach at AŠ Mladá Boleslav and was his primary early mentor in the sport. This is a direct family-domain apprenticeship in javelin throwing.
primary_early_advantage_tags: javelin-thrower parents, father as coach, Dukla military sports club, Czechoslovak athletics tradition, premature birth adversity
evidence_summary: Železný grew up in a javelin-throwing family where both parents competed and his father coached him from the start, providing a textbook family-domain apprenticeship. He won the Czechoslovak junior title at 17 and broke the world record at 21. The Dukla Banská Bystrica military sports club provided an elite training environment. Despite being born prematurely with physical challenges and suffering chronic back problems, he developed exceptional technique that made him the greatest javelin thrower in history. His family domain advantage was unusually strong and directly catalytic.
starting_point: Born prematurely in Mladá Boleslav, Czechoslovakia to parents who were both javelin throwers; father became his coach and introduced him to the sport from childhood.
current_position: Retired from competition in 2006; widely considered the greatest javelin thrower in history with three Olympic golds, three World Championship titles, and the world record of 98.48m; now coaching, including Neeraj Chopra.

trajectory.event: Won Czechoslovak junior javelin title and debuted internationally at the European Junior Championships in Schwechat.
Broke the world record with 87.66m in Nitra and won bronze at the World Championships in Rome.
Won Olympic silver medal at the Seoul Olympics, missing gold by 16 cm.
Won Olympic gold medal at the Barcelona Olympics with an Olympic record of 89.66m.
Set the current world record of 98.48m in Jena and won Olympic gold at Atlanta.
Won third consecutive Olympic gold at Sydney, becoming the only javelin thrower with three Olympic titles.
Retired from competitive athletics after a two-decade career at the top.

name: Sandra Morgan
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold in the 4x100m freestyle relay at the 1956 Melbourne Olympics at age 14, becoming the youngest Australian Olympic gold medalist; also won gold at the 1958 British Empire and Commonwealth Games.
early_history_summary: Born in Tamworth, NSW, Morgan grew up in Punchbowl, a suburb of southwestern Sydney. Her father Barrington, a plumber and former childhood swimmer, vowed she would become a national champion and was her driving force. She learned to swim at Bankstown at age 7, won the district championship at 8, the NSW Primary School championship at 11, and the Australian Junior Championship at 13. In 1956 at age 14, she won Olympic gold in the 4x100m freestyle relay in world record time.
family_context_summary: Born in Tamworth, NSW, and grew up in Punchbowl, Sydney. Father Barrington was a plumber who had been a successful childhood swimmer and vowed his daughter would become a national champion. Oldest of four children.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a plumber but had success as a swimmer in his childhood and became Sandra's driving and inspirational force, vowing she would become a national champion. This represents a family-domain transfer of swimming aspiration and basic knowledge.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father's swimming ambition, Bankstown Pool training, Australian swimming system, Dawn Fraser teammates, early competitive immersion
evidence_summary: Morgan's father, a plumber and former childhood swimmer, was her driving force, vowing she would become a national champion. She learned to swim at 7 at Bankstown Pool and progressed rapidly through the Australian swimming development system. By 14 she was the youngest Olympic gold medalist in Australian history, swimming alongside legends Dawn Fraser and Lorraine Crapp. Her father's swimming background and the strong Australian swimming ecosystem were the key advantages; the family was working-class with no financial platform.
starting_point: Born in Tamworth, NSW, Australia to a plumber father who had been a successful childhood swimmer; grew up in Punchbowl, a working-class suburb of southwestern Sydney.
current_position: Retired from competitive swimming in December 1960 at age 18; ran a swim school at Bonnet Bay for 15 years; awarded the Australian Sports Medal in 2000; now in her 80s.

trajectory.event: Won the Australian Junior Championship for 110 yards freestyle.
Won Olympic gold in the 4x100m freestyle relay at the Melbourne Olympics, becoming the youngest Australian Olympic gold medalist.
Won gold in the 4x110 yards freestyle relay at the British Empire and Commonwealth Games in Cardiff.
Competed at the Rome Olympics and retired from competitive swimming in December 1960.
Participated in the Sydney 2000 Olympic Torch relay and received the Australian Sports Medal.
